terms.gloss: grammar; the study of language and of the poets
evidence: Cic. Fin. 3.5: ut ipsa philosophia, ut rhētorica, dialectica, grammatica (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: One of the Greek words that Cicero says use has made Latin (Fin. 3.5). Roman grammar took in more than rules: Quintilian divides it into correct speech and the explanation of the poets (1.4.2). Grammatical is grammaticus; according to the rules, grammaticē (Quint. 1.6.27).
Quintilian’s form of the word, declined in Greek.
Ars alone is a grammar book, like Donatus’s Ars; Traupman gives ars for a textbook (p. 32).

terms.gloss: grammar, the first teaching of letters
evidence: Quint. 2.1.4: grammaticē (quam in Latīnum trānsferentēs litterātūram vocāvērunt)
terms.comment: The Latin rendering of grammaticē, from litterae; in Seneca the first teaching of letters to children. In modern Latin it is literature.

phrases.latin: haec igitur professiō, cum brevissimē in duās partēs dīvidātur, rēctē loquendī scientiam et poētārum ēnarrātiōnem, plūs habet in recessū quam fronte prōmittit
phrases.english: This profession, then, though in the briefest terms it divides into two parts, the science of speaking correctly and the explanation of the poets, has more behind it than it shows in front

phrases.latin: aliud esse Latīnē aliud grammaticē loquī
phrases.english: speaking Latin is one thing, speaking grammar another
